articles.title: This is how you should store your air conditioner in the winter, according to HVAC experts
articles.summary: Removing your air conditioner from the window for winter can help prevent freezing temperatures and excess moisture from ruining it. HVAC experts share exactly how you should store it.
articles.body: With all the content available online these days, it can be hard to figure out what’s real and what’s hype. While we don’t always have the answers, we have a direct line to people who do — which is why we present to you our series The Internet Made Me Ask, where we have experts break down the truth about some of the buzziest trends on our timelines, like whether jazz shoes are bad for your feet. Fall has officially arrived, and with the cooler air (in most states) comes a fresh round of seasonal chores. Outdoor furniture gets covered up, sweaters come out of storage, and your window air conditioner needs to come out of the window. If that last task isn’t on your list, it should be. According to Josh Mitchell, an HVAC technician and owner of Air Conditioner Lab, a site that helps consumers get information on HVAC issues, leaving your unit in place all winter can shorten its lifespan. But simply yanking it out and tucking it into a closet isn’t the answer either. Cleaning it and storing it the right way, Mitchell says, helps ensure it’s ready to perform when hot weather returns. To help you take down, clean and store your air conditioner properly, I asked HVAC experts for their best advice. Here’s what they recommend. When should you put your air conditioner in storage? There’s no single right date for storing your AC unit; hot sleepers may want to hang on to theirs a little longer, while those who get chilly at night may be ready to take it out sooner. Still, there’s a good benchmark you can follow. “The general rule is that when the outdoor temperature continuously falls below 60 degrees Fahrenheit, you know it is time to turn off your air conditioner,” says Ben Green, an associate at The Chill Brothers, an HVAC service company in Texas. “You probably will not need the air conditioning once it gets that cool, and keeping it on could allow chilly drafts to enter your house.” Don’t wait for the first frost, either, Green adds, since freezing temperatures can damage the unit. How to remove your air conditioner Window air conditioners are bulky, heavy and awkward to maneuver, so taking one out can be a challenge. Once the unit is unplugged, these steps from Green can help make the job go more smoothly: Remove the seals and weather stripping. Anything you used to keep the unit snug in the window can make it stick when you try to pull it out.Take off the brackets. Unscrew or unclip anything holding the unit in place.Tilt it slightly inward. As you lift it, angling the unit toward the room keeps leftover water from splashing back into your home.Watch the frame and sill. Lift carefully so the unit doesn’t bang into either one, which can cause damage to your AC and the window it’s in.Set it on a towel. Any remaining water will drip out, so let the towel catch it. What products can you use to clean an air conditioner? Below I share some tips on how to clean your air conditioner before you store it, so you’ll want to gather some of these cleaning supplies before you dive into the process. While you can certainly use a damp cloth and some soap and water, the experts I spoke with say there are also a handful of products on the market that can help you get the job done. These soft, lint-free microfiber cloths are scratch-free and highly absorbent, making them a gentle way to clean delicate surfaces — including wiping down your air conditioner’s filter or the outside of the unit. Each cloth is machine washable, so it holds up to repeated use. The color-coded pack makes it easy to keep one cloth for your air conditioner and others for other jobs. NBC Selected senior editor Shalwah Evans has them and she says she uses them to clean so many things around the home. “I wipe the dust from my air vents and furniture with these, not to mention they’re great for washing dishes and wiping windows and mirrors without leaving streaks and lint on glass,” she says. Frost King’s foaming coil cleaner dissolves dirt, grease and oil from air conditioner coils, fan blades and reusable filters. The water-based formula is low-VOC, lemon-scented, needs no rinsing (just a simple wipe) and has a 360-degree valve that sprays at any angle to reach tight spots. It also helps neutralize odors from standing water in drain pans. This gives you everything to restore an air conditioner’s coils and vents — including small brushes that slip between grates and firm-bristled brushes that work well on coils. There is also a curved brush that reaches deep inside the unit, scrubbing condenser fins without damaging the coils. It’s worth noting that while some dirt may come off if you use the brushes dry, using a bit of soap and water or a coil cleaner in conjunction with the brushes will allow them to be most effective. How to clean your air conditioner before storing it Once the unit is out of the window, give it a good cleaning before it goes into storage. It’s a key step for two reasons. “Dust and debris left on your air conditioner can reduce its efficiency when you go to restart it in the summer,” says Green. “Plus, if you put your AC away with water in it, mold could grow and nobody wants to inhale that when you turn it back on.” The good news is that the job is relatively easy. “Simply wipe down the outside of it well and remember to clean or change the air filter,” says Green. If you see dirt on the coils, he adds, you can vacuum them or clean them lightly. Mitchell recommends washing the filter with a mild solution of soap and water. You can also use the products we mention above to ensure a thorough cleaning. Finally, make sure everything is completely dry before you pack the unit away. Wipe down any spots that look damp, then let it sit in a cool, dry place until you’re certain no moisture remains. How to store your air conditioner Your AC is out of the window and clean, which means it’s finally ready to go into hibernation until warm weather returns. If you still have the original box, that’s the best place for it, says Green. No box? Wrap the unit in plastic instead. Either way, you’ll keep out dampness, dust and critters, he adds. Just make sure the unit sits upright, the same way it does in a window. “This is crucial because any residual fluids from tipping it could damage interior compartments,” says Green. Next comes choosing the right spot. “Select a location that is dry and away from very hot or cold temperatures,” says Mitchell. “A garage, cellar, or even a closet are the ideal spaces. Just stay away from sheds and attics that could get extremely damp or cold in the winter. The worst thing for your unit is moisture, as it can cause rust and electrical damage.” Meet our HVAC experts At NBC Select, we work with experts with specialized knowledge and authority based on relevant training and experience. We also ensure all expert advice and recommendations are made independently and without undisclosed financial conflicts of interest. Josh Mitchell is an HVAC technician and owner of the Air Conditioner Lab, a website that helps consumers get answers to HVAC issues. Ben Green is an associate at The Chill Brothers, an HVAC service company in Texas Why trust NBC Selected? I am a commerce editor at NBC Selected and a journalist who regularly covers home, lifestyle and more. I have written about how to keep food fresh during a power outage and whether portable washers and dryers are worth the money. For this story, I interviewed two HVAC experts on how to store your air conditioner during the colder months. articles.title: Venezuela’s opposition leader blocked 3 times from returning to country
articles.summary: Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado was blocked from returning to her country three times over a 24-hour timeframe on Tuesday. “She has attempted to enter the country by air and sea but has been turned away each time,” adviser David Smolansky told The Hill. Machado, the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize recipient, left the country…
articles.body:
Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado was blocked from returning to her country three times over a 24-hour timeframe on Tuesday.

“She has attempted to enter the country by air and sea but has been turned away each time,” adviser David Smolansky told The Hill .

Machado, the 2025 Nobel Peace Prize recipient, left the country under the protection of a U.S. rescue team last December. She appeared in public for the first time in 11 months in Oslo, Norway, hours after her daughter accepted the Nobel Peace Prize on her mother’s behalf.

Machado attempted to return home after 7.5- and 7.2-magnitude earthquakes hit several Venezuelan states, including the capital city of Caracas, in June. President Trump discouraged her from going amid developing relations with Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodríguez. Machado accused the Venezuelan government of preventing her return.

The opposition leader worked to certify Venezuela’s 2024 presidential election results to prove that fellow opposition leader Edmundo González won against President Nicolás Maduro amid allegations of widespread election fraud. The ensuing crackdown prompted Machado to go into hiding.

Machado has vowed to return to her country and run for president if her country holds elections before the end of 2026, after U.S. forces captured Maduro in early January. She told other opposition leaders in Panama that they remain committed to Venezuela’s transition of power and to holding free and fair elections.

“I will be president when the time comes. But it doesn’t matter. That should be decided in elections by the Venezuelan people,” Machado said in an interview with CBS News’s “Face the Nation” in February.

Trump has praised Rodríguez, saying she wants to “make Venezuela great again.” But Republican lawmakers have opposed the interim leader, with Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) calling Rodríguez a “necessary evil.”

The U.S. and Venezuela reached a major oil deal , one that Trump described as “THE BIGGEST OIL DEAL IN WORLD HISTORY!” Rodríguez granted a joint venture between the U.S. government and North American Blue Energy Partners, a private company that is Venezuela’s second-largest private oil producer, with 100-year “concessions” for oil fields containing 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, about 21 percent of Venezuela’s total estimated oil.

As part of the deal, the Trump administration said that the U.S. will get the right to purchase 20 percent of the oil that North American Blue Energy Partners unearths at the cost of production. This oil will go toward the U.S.’s Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which has seen its stockpile diminish in response to the Russia-Ukraine war and the U.S.-Israeli conflict with Iran.

articles.title: Iran’s president laid out Tehran’s demands to the world, from a podium in New York
articles.summary: Seven months after the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran, the Iranian president stood on a podium in New York to tell President Donald Trump that the Islamic Republic “will not bow down.”
articles.body: Seven months after the United States and Israel launched a war on Iran, the Iranian president stood on a podium in New York to tell President Donald Trump that the Islamic Republic “will not bow down.” As his country confronts its gravest existential war, and amid Trump’s threats of “annihilation” and mounting economic strain at home, Iran’s Masoud Pezeshkian told world leaders attending the United Nations General Assembly that Iran will not yield on its nuclear program, missile defenses or control of the Strait of Hormuz, the vital waterway through which a fifth of the world’s oil once flowed. “We cannot let some have free access and gain their interest from a waterway while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggressions upon us, to impose insecurity upon us, to forbid us access to our own waterways,” Pezeshkian said. The Iranian president used the world stage to deliver Tehran’s demands and Iran’s core message to Trump, who has sought through war to defeat the Islamic Republic. Trump has boasted that the United States has “blown up” nuclear sites in Iran, and he has claimed control over the Strait of Hormuz. From the same podium on Tuesday, he said he was considering whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic” and drive it “into hell.” Pezeshkian’s address was among the most anticipated speeches at this year’s United Nations gathering, and delivering it on American soil was a rare historic moment: a foreign leader holding forth in an enemy country still at war with his own. Despite Washington’s early forecasts that the fighting would be brief, the US-Israeli war on Iran has instead dragged on, turning a military operation that began with the killing of the Islamic Republic’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, into months of regional instability and one of the defining foreign policy legacies of Trump’s presidency. One of Pezeshkian’s key messages offered a glimpse into how the Islamic Republic seeks to set its postwar regional stance, telling Iran’s neighbors that its future security must be guaranteed or the entire region will have to “live under insecurity together.” The message carried an implicit threat, according to one expert. “Iran was presenting regional security as indivisible, signaling that continued pressure and conflict would impose costs across the region,” Sanam Vakil, director of the Middle East and North Africa program at London’s Chatham House think tank, told CNN. But the message also signals that Iran knows it will need to find a way to coexist with the rest of the region, according to another expert, Hamidreza Azizi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group. “This reflects an understanding that, at the end of the day, Iran will need to find an arrangement for peaceful coexistence with its neighbors,” Azizi said. New diplomatic framework Pezeshkian delivered his speech at the UN a day after Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi held at least two hours of talks in New York with Trump’s peace envoy Steve Witkoff, the first sign of diplomacy between the two nations since an ill-fated agreement was signed more than three months ago. Following Pezeshkian’s remarks, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said those talks did not yield any major breakthrough, indicating the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) from earlier this year was no longer on the cards. A plan in June for further negotiations between Iran and the United States never came to fruition. The conflict flared instead, leaving the region sinking deeper into uncertainty over how the war would end. At home, Pezeshkian and the Iranian officials who engaged Washington diplomatically have faced scrutiny from rival hard-line factions, which regard any agreement with Trump as tantamount to surrender. “The foreign minister must explain on which authorization was his meeting with the representative of the aggressor enemy conducted?” Ebrahim Rezaei, a hard-line lawmaker, asked Wednesday after Araghchi met Witkoff. Pezeshkian has also drawn criticism from hard-liners for attending the meeting in New York. “His critics expressed concern that if … he signaled any intention to compromise to the outside world, this would be interpreted as a sign of weakness and desperation and would therefore be counterproductive for Iran, which wants to end the war on its own terms,” Azizi of the Crisis Group said. As Pezeshkian and Araghchi delivered Iran’s demands to the world and a message of coexistence to the region, security officials back home announced a more hard-line position in Iran’s negotiating tactics. Iran’s Supreme National Security Council chief, Mohsen Rezaei, told state media in an interview broadcast around the same time as Pezeshkian’s speech that the Islamic Republic will adopt a new framework when negotiating with the US that will require Washington to take the first step. “Under this new framework, the era of rhetoric and negotiations for their own sake has come to an end,” Rezaei said in the interview. “Any future talks, or the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, will be contingent upon Washington’s full implementation of Iran’s requirements as a precondition.” His remarks perhaps not only sent a message to Washington but were also aimed at assuaging hard-liners skeptical of the Iranian officials negotiating in New York. Yet as Iran conducted diplomacy at the UN and signaled future coexistence with the region, Oman’s Maritime Security Center said a ship was targeted near the Strait of Hormuz, killing one person. “Vessels are advised to transit with caution,” the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) center said.

articles.title: Tap water on paper, no proper accounts, says J&K  probe panel
articles.summary: SRINAGAR: Tap water existing only on paper, people in some areas still having to hire horses for “transporting drinking water to their houses”, water
articles.body: SRINAGAR: Tap water existing only on paper, people in some areas still having to hire horses for “transporting drinking water to their houses”, water pipes abandoned and littered around at some places are some of the damning observations in the report by a J&K assembly committee that was formed to probe alleged irregularities in the implementation of the Rs 13,000-crore Jal Jeevan Mission scheme in the union territory announced by PM Modi on Aug 15, 2019, with a target of completing it by 2024.The 13-member committee, formed on April 9, 2024, following widespread allegations of irregularities in the implementation of the scheme, tabled its report in the J&K House on Monday.As per the report, overall target achievement of work execution across the union territory was still 37.28 percent.Most of the JJM schemes in Udhampur are “classic examples of good paper work, contrary to field work and ground situation,” it said. “Most of the schemes in Poonch exist on papers.”The report also said that there is no credible record at least produced before the House committee as regards details of water pipes procured, utilized, and left unutilized. “During on-spot visits by the committee water pipes were found abandoned and littered around.”It also said Panchayati Raj institutions were excluded from implementation of the scheme.The JJM scheme aims to provide potable drinking water in taps to all rural homes by 2024. Around 3,253 water supply schemes have been sanctioned in J&K at a cost of about Rs 13,000 crore.JJM is a 90:10 funding scheme between the Centre and the J&K govt.Officials of the Jal Shakti department said implementation was delayed in J&K as little progress could be made in the initial months following the abrogation of Article 370 on August 5, 2019. They said the administrative transition took about five months, followed by the COVID-19 pandemic, further delaying implementation.The department told the committee that the model and methods used to implement the JJM in the rest of the country could not be replicated in J&K due to its “difficult geography, limited road connectivity and lack of locally available skilled manpower.” It said the tendering process began picking up pace only after 2022.Ajaz Ahmad Jan, one of the committee members, said despite huge investment, a majority of rural households, especially in Rajouri and Poonch, are still facing hardships in fetching safe drinking water and there has been no benefit of the scheme.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Heads of AI firms tell UN Security Council that it could be a risk to all humanity
articles.summary: The heads of major artificial intelligence firms pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to save the world or at least its people — in the form of someh...
articles.body:
UNITED NATIONS (AP) — The heads of major artificial intelligence firms pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to save the world or at least its people — in the form of somehow regulating the burgeoning technology that they have been designing.

"If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," said Dario Amodei, chief executive officer of Anthropic. And from his competitor Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, came this assessment: "We could lose control of the future to AI."

Both said the countries of the world, through the U.N. Security Council, where they testified Wednesday, have to set safeguards of some kind, which would be actual controls to prevent the technology from getting too powerful to rein in.

They also called for the world to make sure that the power of AI isn't concentrated in one company or country. They said that as they also touted the benefits of the technology for bettering humanity and what Altman called "giving people more power over their own lives."

Those tech leaders "are telling us in stark terms that it cannot be left to them to prevent disaster from befalling the world," said United Kingdom Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said at the Security Council. "We cannot ignore them because they are right.''

AI will be at the heart of G20 discussions

Miliband said when the U.K. takes control of the G20 next year it will put controlling AI at the heart of discussions, looking for a single set of global standards "to insure that AI development is safe."

Worries about control of AI are "not a reason to pause its further development or to constrain it with new global governance structure," said White House Science Adviser Michael Kratsios. "We want you, our allies and partners, to share in the benefits of this technology."

For most of the world leaders, along with California Governor Gavin Newsom in New York for climate discussions, one of the key questions about AI is this: Who should control life-and-death decisions — human or machine?

Amodei, Altman and Hugging Face CEO Clément Delangue, who spoke via a glitchy remote connection, spoke with the U.N.'s most powerful council because they and world leaders are trying to figure out not just whether to control AI, but by who, how it could possibly be done and when it might be just too late.

The day before, U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned of "killer robots." Experts and European leaders said that's not hyperbole but something that's either already a grim reality or perilously close.

Amodei called on the nations of the world to agree on not letting AI build biological weapons, figure out how to verify what models have the capability to do and "establish common standards" for testing and for loss of control and misuse.

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, whose country convened Wednesday's meeting and has fostered various other coalitions and discussions about AI, compared the current state of it to both the runaway computer HAL9000 in the movie "2001: A Space Odyssey" and the dawn of the atomic age.

"Just as with the atom back then, the international community must now regulate AI in order to make the most of its potential and avoid the worst," Barrot said.

Other leaders and nations are paying close attention to AI

His wasn't the only concern expressed during this high-profile U.N. meeting week.

Ukrainian President President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, speaking at the General Assembly, said some kind of human control over machines must achieved soon. Otherwise, he said, for his country it may be just too late.

"There is already a real possibility that AI, not only people, will begin to decide what happens on the battlefield. And we need peace before we reach that point," Zelenskyy said.

Last month, a Russian drone seemingly using AI "autonomously made a targeting decision that killed three Ukrainians. Killer robots are technically easy to build, and they are real. We should not be under any illusions otherwise," said Kentaro Toyama, an information technology professor at the University of Michigan.

The U.N. meeting unfolded as Chinese President Xi Jinping headed to Washington for a much-anticipated state visit. The U.S. and China are jostling for AI dominance, and AI interests are looking to what comes out of Xi's discussions with U.S. President Donald Trump. Ahead of the meeting, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the two countries had discussed a potential new "notification mechanism" for AI incidents that could impact national security.

But on Tuesday, Trump, lauding AI as "superintelligence," said the United States would reject efforts to control the technology as it tries to win the development race with China. Kratsios was the one of the few who used that term in the Security Council.

Meanwhile, regional groups in Europe, Asia and elsewhere also are trying to coordinate AI policies, and various nations — and even subcomponents, such as U.S. states — are crafting their own.

Still, U.N. watchers and risk experts say the world body hasn't been relegated to the sidelines on AI regulation.

"The U.N. is not in the driver's seat of global discussions on AI, but it hasn't been kicked out of the car yet," said Daniel Forti, who oversees U.N. affairs at the International Crisis Group, a think tank.

Farnoush Amiri, Edith M. Lederer and Jennifer McDermott contributed to this report from the United Nations.

articles.title: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years in New York sexual assault retrial
articles.summary: The ruling seals six years of legal battles after Weinstein’s initial conviction for sexually assaulting TV assistant.
articles.body:
Harvey Weinstein , the disgraced movie mogul, has been sentenced in Manhattan to 15 years in prison for a felony sex crime in another #MeToo reckoning.

Weinstein’s sentencing on Wednesday for sexually assaulting one-time TV production assistant Miriam Haley followed a legal odyssey spanning more than six years, when New York’s highest court overturned his 2020 conviction. A second jury found Weinstein guilty again at a retrial last year.

Once among the most powerful figures in the entertainment industry, Weinstein was an Oscar-winning producer whose hits included “Shakespeare in Love,” “Pulp Fiction” and “Chocolat.” But his downfall came quickly after sexual assault allegations in 2017 set off the #MeToo movement.

Weinstein, 74, is expected to appeal and maintains that he never raped or sexually assaulted anyone. He is now likely to remain behind bars well into his 80s. Seated in a wheelchair, he was quickly moved out of the courtroom after the sentencing, while some of his accusers hugged and brushed away tears.

Haley, 49, appeared in court on Wednesday morning and delivered a victim impact statement in which she talked about enduring seven years of public smear campaigns and humiliation orchestrated by Weinstein, his legal team and allegedly paid podcasters aiming to sour her image.

Haley added that her experience following the assault had “already been a life sentence” for her, and implored the judge to take all of this into consideration.

Owing to a cycle of retrials, appeals and judicial proceedings, Weinstein has remained incarcerated since his 2018 arrest and is now serving time in a prison medical ward.

Weinstein, first publicly accused of wrongdoing in 2017, was detained a year later. In 2024, New York’s highest court overturned the original 2020 conviction that had sentenced the former Hollywood producer to 23 years in prison, ruling that the inclusion of extraneous, non-indicted testimony had compromised the equity of the trial.

Prosecutors attempted to retry the case last June, but it ended in a split verdict after the jury foreperson refused to return to deliberate amid a jury room feud. Weinstein was convicted of a first-degree criminal sex act on a separate count at the time, again.

Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate rape case in Los Angeles.

articles.title: Trump administration invites Putin to attend G20 summit in Miami
articles.summary: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio says summit would be opportunity for Russian president to engage with global leaders.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has invited his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin to the upcoming G20 summit in Miami, Florida, the latest step meant to build ties between the two countries amid Russia’s ongoing invasion of Ukraine.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Wednesday that Putin had been invited to travel to the summit in December, saying that he hopes the Russian leader will take the opportunity to meet with global leaders.

“In order to solve problems, you have to meet with the people that you disagree with or the people that you might have some issues with,” Rubio said. “So we’ve invited President Putin to the G20.”

“We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president, but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept,” Rubio said.

Rubio’s remarks followed a meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA), currently convening in New York City.

During a speech to the UNGA on Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called on the world to place more financial pressure on Russia.

“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time. And that is exactly why we insist on limiting trade with the aggressor, and why we are burning Russia’s revenues ourselves,” he said, adding that he is sceptical that Russia is sincerely interested in taking steps that could end the war.

Trump has searched in vain for an agreement between Russia and Ukraine to end the war sparked by Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.

Ukrainian officials have called for a pause on strikes targeting energy infrastructure and for steps to facilitate shipping for the Black Sea. Russia has given little sign that it is interested in such an arrangement.

“We are not going to have a pause in our special military operation,” Lavrov told the UN Security Council on Wednesday, accusing Europe of wanting to pause the fighting in order to “pump the Kyiv regime with weapons”.

Rubio, however, continued to express optimism about the possibility of a temporary ceasefire.

“I think both sides have expressed an interest in some limited ceasefire that involves grain and energy,” he said. “Obviously, you know, that won’t be easy, either.”

Zelenskyy told reporters that Kyiv remains open to a maritime truce in the Black Sea.

“We are waiting for Russia’s response,” he said, adding that his country is ready “to ensure safe shipping and food security in the Black Sea if Russia is ready to take real steps towards de-escalation, too”.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) issued an arrest warrant for Putin in 2023 for the alleged war crime of deportation of Ukrainian children to Russian territory. The arrest warrant obliges member states to arrest Putin if he travels to their countries, but the court has no enforcement mechanism for this. The US is not a member of the ICC.

articles.title: Trump's Board of Peace unveils $2.45bn plan to begin Gaza's reconstruction
articles.summary: The figure was announced during a meeting of the group's board at the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has announced a Gaza recovery plan worth $2.45bn (£1.85bn) during a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.

The funding will be spread across 66 programmes over six months, and directed at housing, diesel generation and waste removal, among other needs.

But the board admitted substantial donations were still needed, with $18bn pledged but only $280m handed over so far. The board estimates full recovery and reconstruction will require about $71.4bn over the next decade.

Jared Kushner, Gaza Executive Board member and Trump's son-in-law, conceded the project faced "different delays on different things, for whatever reason".

"The goal of today was really just to show you that we're really fully committed to doing it," he told the meeting of board members and stakeholders.

He was joined in New York by US envoy Steve Witkoff, who said the group had made "real progress" over the past year.

"All of the hostages are home. There is a ceasefire, imperfect as it may be, but it still exists. Humanitarian efforts have achieved historic results, with billions of dollars donated and pledged to meet urgent needs and support the long work of recovery," Witkoff added.

In addition to fundraising, the plan faces significant challenges including how to ensure security for those operating in Gaza, overhaul internal governance and find consensus between Israeli and Palestinians officials.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a separate press conference on Wednesday that "a number of countries have stepped forward and pledged financial assistance" and the board was "looking for more that will participate in that".

Michael Eisenberg, an Israeli-American Board of Peace member, told the BBC's Newshour programme what the next steps were likely to be.

"Because it's a war zone, you need to remove unexploded ordnance. And then there are still hundreds of kilometres of tunnels underneath Gaza which need to be destroyed as well.

"Once that's all done, Gazans can get to rebuilding again: whether it's housing, or better sanitation, or other things," Eisenberg said.

In August, a senior official on the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, criticised Israel's continuing air strikes on Gaza , as well as the actions of Hamas.

In August, Mladenov warned that a collapse of last October's ceasefire would be "a point of no return" for the region.

At least 1,381 Palestinians, including 300 children, have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the US-brokered ceasefire began, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The Israeli military says five of its soldiers have been killed in combat since the ceasefire and one contractor was killed in an "operational accident".

The Board of Peace was created as part of Donald Trump's 20-point Gaza peace plan, which he unveiled alongside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in September last year.

Hamas agreed to return all 48 remaining hostages being held in Gaza in exchange for Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails and Gaza detainees, and to the idea of handing over the governance of Gaza to Palestinian technocrats.

In July, Hamas said it had accepted a disarmament plan for Gaza which will see it lay down its arms, provided Israel ends "all forms of aggression" and withdraws its forces from Gaza.

But that was later rejected by Netanyahu, who said the military would stay in Gaza until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.

The Board of Peace was originally thought to be an international organisation intended to bring peace to Gaza, but later expanded to include conflicts worldwide.

articles.title: Tanzania began restoring the Mpiji River after years of deforestation; native trees are being planted to rebuild wildlife habitat
articles.summary: Tanzania has begun restoring the Mpiji River through a community-driven project focused on rebuilding native vegetation and wildlife habitat after years
articles.body: Tanzania has begun restoring the Mpiji River through a community-driven project focused on rebuilding native vegetation and wildlife habitat after years of environmental neglect and deforestation. The initiative centres on planting indigenous tree species, rehabilitating land and increasing local biodiversity around the river. According to the Institute of Environment, Climate and Development Sustainability (IECDS), native vegetation is intended to improve resilience to local climate conditions, provide better habitats for wildlife, support ecological balance, sequester carbon and stabilise soil. Funded by NCBA Bank Tanzania, the 12-month project has four objectives: ecosystem restoration, community engagement, biodiversity enhancement and climate change mitigation.How can native trees restore wildlife habitat along the Mpiji RiverA central part of the Mpiji River restoration project is the planting of native tree species. The use of indigenous vegetation is intended to help restored areas become more resilient to local climate conditions while providing better habitats for wildlife and maintaining ecological balance. The tree planting is therefore being carried out as part of wider efforts to rebuild vegetation around the river.The restoration work is also intended to address environmental pressures linked to climate change. Native vegetation can help sequester carbon and stabilise soil, while the wider project aims to improve the landscape and support biodiversity. The initiative combines tree planting with land rehabilitation rather than focusing on vegetation alone.What are the four goals of the Mpiji River restoration projectThe project is funded by NCBA Bank Tanzania and is planned for 12 months. The initiative has four specific objectives: “Ecosystem restoration, Community Engagement, Biodiversity Enhancement and Climate Change mitigation”. These objectives provide the framework for the restoration activities being carried out around the Mpiji River.The biodiversity component is linked to the restoration of habitats and the use of native vegetation. Indigenous trees can provide better habitats for wildlife while helping to maintain ecological balance. The project consequently connects the recovery of vegetation around the river with efforts to enhance biodiversity in the surrounding environment.How are local communities involved in the Mpiji River restorationThe Mpiji River initiative is implemented as a community-led environmental restoration project. The approach demonstrates how environmental restoration can be pursued through “grassroots engagement and ecological knowledge”. The organisation describes community involvement as central to aligning environmental objectives with local needs. The project offers a model that can be replicated in other regions facing similar environmental challenges. articles.title: Indian-origin man in Canada, a permanent resident, jailed for sexually assaulting 15-year-old loses bid to avoid deportation
articles.summary: A Canadian permanent resident originally from Punjab has been sentenced to 15 months in prison after a judge rejected his request for a shorter sentence
articles.body: A Canadian permanent resident originally from Punjab has been sentenced to 15 months in prison after a judge rejected his request for a shorter sentence that could have helped him preserve his right to appeal a possible deportation order.Harpreet Singh, 30, was convicted in Ontario of sexual interference, making sexually explicit material available to a child for the purpose of facilitating sexual interference, and exposing a person under 16 to sexual activity for a sexual purpose.Singh, who was born and raised in Punjab, India, had asked the court to sentence him to 182 days in jail followed by two years of probation. His immigration lawyer argued that a sentence of six months or more on any individual count could have serious immigration consequences for him.The lawyer told the court that Singh could lose his right to appeal a removal order to Canada's Immigration Appeal Division if sentenced to six months or more, potentially preventing him from seeking discretionary relief on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.But Ontario Court of Justice Justice Joe Patrick Paul Fiorucci rejected the request, saying immigration consequences could not justify imposing a sentence that would otherwise be inappropriate.“Such a sentence would be neither fit nor proportionate,” the judge said in his September 15 decision, according to the National Post.Instead, Singh was sentenced to 15 months in prison followed by three years of probation.What happened to the teenage girl?The court heard that Singh encountered the 15-year-old girl on a city bus on May 1, 2023.Singh sat across from the girl during the journey and watched sexually explicit material on his phone, according to the court decision.The two strangers got off the bus at the same location at about 11:23pm.According to the judgment, Singh followed the girl onto a dark trail, grabbed her from behind by the collar and hair and then exposed himself while holding his phone and displaying sexually explicit material to her.The teenager fought back by elbowing and pushing Singh before fleeing.The girl's identity is protected by a publication ban.The court said she described the incident as “humiliating, terrifying, and deeply violating” and said it had changed her sense of safety in her community.She experienced anxiety, panic and fear in places where she had previously felt comfortable, according to the judgment.Judge rejects immigration-based sentencing requestSingh's lawyer argued that a sentence of less than six months could have significant consequences for his immigration status.The judge said he had considered those consequences but rejected the argument that they should determine the sentence. "While immigration consequences are entitled to serious consideration, they cannot be permitted to dominate the sentencing exercise or create a separate sentencing regime for offenders facing possible removal from Canada,” Fiorucci said.The judge described Singh's conduct as deliberate and predatory and said the offences were directed at a vulnerable child.He said the circumstances were “highly aggravating” and that Singh's degree of moral blameworthiness was high.The Crown had sought between 12 and 15 months in prison, along with three years of probation.Singh's background and rehabilitationSingh was single and had no children at the time of sentencing. His family had been arranging a marriage for him, but those plans were put on hold while his criminal case was being resolved.He was unemployed when he was sentenced but was looking for work, particularly in the electrical field. He had also volunteered in his religious community for several years.Family members and a friend submitted letters describing him as honest, hardworking, respectful, dependable and supportive.The judge noted that Singh had undergone counselling with a social worker. According to the court, the treatment helped him understand the seriousness and consequences of his conduct, accept responsibility, identify relevant risk factors and understand the importance of boundaries and continued self-monitoring.A social worker assessed Singh as currently presenting a low risk of sexual reoffending, taking into account factors including his status as a first-time offender and his participation in treatment.However, the judge said the seriousness of the offences and the harm suffered by the victim required a substantial custodial sentence.Singh will serve 15 months in prison followed by three years of probation.You use AI every day. articles.title: Idaho officials identify 1982 suicide victim, seek out potential connection to Tylenol murders
articles.summary: Idaho investigators announced Wednesday they had identified a man who died in a Boise church more than 40 years ago, and they believe he could be connected to the 1982 Tylenol murders in Chicago.
articles.body: Idaho investigators announced Wednesday they had identified a man who died in a Boise church more than 40 years ago, and they believe he could be connected to the 1982 Tylenol murders in Chicago. The man at the center of the cold case, referred to for years as “Unknown Wanderer,” died by suicide inside Sacred Heart Catholic Church in Boise on Dec. 4, 1982. The cause of death was determined to be death by cyanide poisoning, according to the Ada County Sheriff’s Office. The wanderer case was reopened in 2019 and detectives renewed efforts to identify him, who had no identification on him when he was found. When re-examining the evidence, a detective found an engraved key among the wanderer’s belongings that led him to a residence in Jacksonville, Florida. Detective Tim Cooper, who works in the sheriff’s cold case unit, was able to identify the man as Dr. Mathew Betkouski. Betkouski worked in two drugstores and those who knew him said he had a “history of volatility,” according to the sheriff’s office. Colleagues have recalled Betkouski as having a fascination with the “perfect crime” and with cyanide as a method to kill without detection, the sheriff’s office said. Cooper also reviewed thousands of documents, including Betkouski’s personal writings. The sheriff’s office believed that Betkouski could have been involved in the 1982 Tylenol poisonings, in which seven people died after taking extra-strength Tylenol capsules laced with cyanide. There has been no evidence so far connecting Betkouski to the Chicago area where the murders occurred at the time. Betkouski had lifelong struggles with mental illness, Cooper said at a news conference Wednesday. He came from a prominent Los Angeles family and was a chemist who “struggled to connect with people.” He suffered a traumatic brain injury in 1974, which Cooper said “caused some of his problems to manifest in more concerning ways than they had before.” He worked at a flavors and fragrances company in Florida for three years starting in 1975, but left to undergo psychiatric treatment in Los Angeles in 1978 after co-workers reported concerning behavior. He returned to the job after a couple of months but was ultimately let go because his situation had not seemed to change. Betkouski’s personal writings included musings about how to manage schizophrenia and depression as well as thoughts of violence, according to Cooper. Betkouski’s brother kept some of his personal items. Among the items found in his desk was a map of Chicago and cyanide, which seemed to be homemade. “This was sodium cyanide,” Cooper said. “This was not potassium cyanide, as was used in the Chicago-area deaths in 1982.” Photos also showed that Betkouski did visit the Chicago area in 1981, a year before the Tylenol deaths. Cooper said it is unclear if Betkouski returned to Chicago the following year. “So where this leaves us is: While our office may have identified some possible connection between Dr. Betkouski and the 1982 events, we’re not naming him as a suspect and we cannot say he was in Chicago in the final week of September 1982,” he said. Information on the case was turned over to Chicago and Arlington Heights police departments. The Arlington Heights Police Department said it continues to work with law enforcement partners in its effort to identify whoever is responsible for the Tylenol murders. It went on to say that it received and reviewed the information provided by the sheriff’s department but did not have additional information to release. The Arlington Heights police statement noted that it “remains an active investigation.” The Chicago Police Department said in a statement that it has been in contact with the Ada County Sheriff’s Office regarding its investigation. It also noted that the Tylenol murders remain an open cold case. An inquiry to the Illinois State Police was referred to the FBI field office in Chicago. The FBI noted that over the past 44 years there have been repeated allegations of links to the murders “which have remain unsubstantiated.” “Out of respect for the ongoing, legitimate investigation, those impacted by the tragedy, and the law enforcement partners who have provided genuine support since the start, the FBI remains the lead on investigating and releasing credible information to the public once the evidence yields a true case resolution,” the FBI statement said. In a news release, Cooper said the department hoped that getting Betkouski’s story out would generate new leads. “I’m especially interested in learning more about his movements between Oct. 15 and Dec. 4, 1982,” he said. Cooper worked with a forensic psychiatrist Dr. Park Dietz, who believes that Betkouski could be “a viable suspect” in the Tylenol murders. The sheriff’s office case will be featured in an “Unsolved Mysteries” documentary on Oct. 9 that will air on The Roku Channel. Investigators have long believed the Tylenol poisonings were committed by man named James Lewis, who died in 2023 without ever being charged in the case. Lewis was convicted of writing ransom notes to Johnson & Johnson, the company that manufactures Tylenol, in an extortion attempt. Jeremy Margolis, a former U.S. attorney and former director of the Illinois State Police, has long named Lewis as a prime suspect in the case. He described the potential Betkouski connection as “utter nonsense” to NBC Chicago. The evidence that pointed to Lewis included the note he wrote to Johnson & Johnson, which demanded $1 million to “stop the killings” as well as drawings he made. Lewis had a pencil drawing to show how a killer could have split the capsules and used a peg board to replace the medicinal powder with cyanide, the station reported.

articles.title: Gaza flotilla activist on hunger strike in Tunisia jail ‘on verge of death’
articles.summary: Wael Naouar has been hospitalised as his hunger strike enters its 39th day, the Gaza Sumud Flotilla says.
articles.body:
Gaza solidarity activist Wael Naouar has been admitted to hospital more than a month after launching a hunger strike to protest his detention in Tunisia, according to the Gaza Sumud Flotilla organisation to which he belongs.

Bassem Trifi, the head of the Tunisian League for the Defence of Human ⁠⁠Rights (LTDH), on Wednesday said Naouar was “in a very critical health condition and on the ⁠⁠verge of death”.

A prison spokesperson did not immediately comment on Naouar’s case and condition. The hunger striker has demanded that authorities drop charges of financial misconduct against him and three other activists.

The four, including Ghassen Henchiri, Ghassen Boughdiri and Nabil Channoufi, were arrested in March after being accused of misusing funds raised for the Global Sumud Flotilla , an international campaign seeking to challenge Israel’s blockade of Gaza. They remain in pre-trial detention.

“Wael Naouar is in hospital, and Tunisian authorities are refusing to disclose any information with his family or lawyers”, the Gaza Sumud Flotilla said in a statement on X.

“This comes right after a judge REJECTED the appeal against the extension of the Sumud 4’s pre-trial detention,” read the statement, which added that the activist was on day 39 of his hunger strike.

The pro-Palestinian activist had lost more than 20kg (44lb) and was suffering from pain throughout his body, according to his lawyer.

None of the activists have been convicted of an offence, but remain under investigation over alleged “suspicious financial flows”.

On Saturday , at least 11 people were arrested in Tunisia after participating in a protest demanding the release of the jailed activists.

The Gaza-bound flotilla set sail last September and was intercepted by Israel, which then detained and deported the activists to the North African country.

Ghassen Bouaazi, a member of the National Committee for the Defence of Sumud Flotilla Activists, said Naouar has recently experienced repeated fainting, difficulty breathing and hallucinations.

“There is now a real danger threatening him,” Bouaazi told Al Jazeera on the sidelines of Saturday’s protest.

A Human Rights Watch report said it had documented what it described as the “weaponisation” of financial and criminal investigations by Tunisian authorities against civil society activists.

The government denies the prosecutions are political, and ‌President Kais Saied says freedoms are guaranteed, the judiciary is independent and, no one is above the law.

articles.title: LoP's presence in panel to pick CEC, ECs 'ornamental': SC judge
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Deliberating on the validity of the law on appointment of chief election commissioner and election commissioners by a panel of the PM, a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Deliberating on the validity of the law on appointment of chief election commissioner and election commissioners by a panel of the PM, a cabinet minister and the leader of opposition, Justice Dipankar Datta on Wednesday pointed out drawbacks and said it gave "overwhelming" power to the executive and made the presence of the LoP "ornamental", undermining the appearance of independence in the selection process. He also noted that since independence, govts had tried to control the poll body."Over seven decades, every dispensation wresting office found it convenient to keep institutions which the Constitution envisioned to be independent under their control. To enact a law on the lines empowered by Article 324(2) would have meant freeing the ECI from exclusive executive control and inviting trouble for the ruling regime. To the mind of this court, this has not been the failing of any one party or one period. A consistent trait of political power, discernible over the decades, has been to preserve leverage over the very body that is meant to judge its claim to power," Justice Datta said.He said if free and fair elections were to be ensured, it was axiomatic that the EC must not only be an independent body but also be seen to act independently and it was "painful to note that not a single party in power, entrusted by the people of India to govern this great nation", took the initiative of enacting a law of the nature which Article 324(2) left to the supreme law-making body, ie Parliament, to legislate."Placing its own electoral fortunes in the hands of a truly independent arbiter was not favoured by any political party, for obvious reasons. To remain in power, the consistent pursuit through executive action has indeed been simple - influence the composition of the EC, control the process of appointment of CEC and ECs and, thereby, temper adverse electoral outcomes," Justice Datta said.Summarising the contentions raised against the law, he added, "The bottom line of the argument runs thus: it would not be a fallacious metaphor if it is said that since the umpire is picked by the captain of one side in a cricket match and his team wins, even if the decisions taken by such umpire are correct, it has the patina of suspicion, for, at the end of the day, the umpire has effectively been chosen by the winning captain."Justice Datta further said, "There can be no gainsaying that free and fair elections, to a large extent, depend on a truly independent EC. It is not enough for the EC to be independent, it must also appear to be independent. The minister nominated by the prime minister, to function as the third member on the selection committee chaired by the prime minister, cannot be expected to defy his own nominator. In such a circumstance, the inclusion of a minister in the selection committee fails to provide the independent counterweight that a neutral selector could and he would merely echo the voice of his leader; and, consequently, the presence of the leader of opposition in the selection committee becomes largely ornamental, without furthering the purpose of his inclusion."Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A South Dakota collector paid $750 for an old crock more than 30 years ago; a $32,000 sale revealed he had its rare twin
articles.summary: More than 30 years ago, a South Dakota collector who goes only by Rick paid $750 for a 30-gallon Red Wing stoneware crock at an auction, storing it in an
articles.body: More than 30 years ago, a South Dakota collector who goes only by Rick paid $750 for a 30-gallon Red Wing stoneware crock at an auction, storing it in an old granary on his farm, where it sat largely forgotten for decades. It wasn't until he saw photos of a nearly identical crock selling for $32,000 in January that he realised what he had. Here's how a routine farm auction find turned into a rare twin to one of the most talked-about crocks in the antiques world.The South Dakota collector's $750 crock discoveryRick's crock, double-stamped, salt-glazed, and decorated with the same hand-painted cobalt butterfly pattern found on the famous $32,000 piece, had spent decades in storage on his farm after his original $750 purchase. When he recognised the resemblance from news photos, he called Nebraska auctioneer Ken Bramer directly. "A guy from up by Watertown, South Dakota, called me and said, 'I got the fourth crock,'" Bramer told Cowboy State Daily. "He said, 'That one you sold down there for such big money? I got the twin sister to it.'" By the next morning, Rick had driven 400 miles overnight to reach Bramer's driveway by 8am.How the $32,000 sale to Lois Jurgens set off "crock mania"The story traces back to a small-town auction in Holdrege, Nebraska, in January, where a crock that had sat on 91-year-old Lois Jurgens' porch for four decades, one she'd considered selling at a garage sale for as little as $50, instead became the centre of a bidding war. According to the New York Post, Jurgens couldn't even attend the auction herself, since it fell on her 91st birthday and she was volunteering at her local church; by the time she arrived at the fairgrounds, a fierce three-way fight between bidders from Texas, Kansas and Iowa had already pushed the price to $32,000. Auctioneer Ken Bramer, who had only jokingly told her beforehand they'd "done a little better than $100," said Jurgens went weak in the knees and had to be helped onto the stage when she learned the final figure. Jurgens told journalist Colleen Williams it was, in all her 91 years, about the most exciting thing that had ever happened to her.Meeting Rick: The twin crock's journey to auctionRick's crock does carry one flaw the original doesn't, a crack down the back, which he said he bought that way. Alongside it, he also brought an 18-inch Red Wing bowl so rare it doesn't appear in standard collector guides. Both pieces are headed to auction on 18 April at the Phelps County fairgrounds in Holdrege, the same venue where Jurgens' crock sold. Like the Kansas collector who placed the winning $32,000 bid while out pheasant hunting, Rick has chosen to stay anonymous, telling Bramer he doesn't want people knowing what he has or where to find him.What experts say drives the growing interest in Red Wing potteryCollectors believe as many as six of these specific decorated crocks exist, with three previously well known among insiders before Rick's emerged as a fourth. Red Wing expert Larry Peterson, who has collected the pottery for 55 years and co-authored three books on the subject, said interest has spread to related pieces like decorated beehive jugs. Peterson doubts Rick's cracked crock will match $32,000 given its condition, but expects strong interest regardless. Since the Jurgens sale, Bramer said he has fielded thousands of calls, texts and emails from people asking whether their own crocks might be valuable, managing to respond to around 250 so far.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tories would prevent long-term jobless spending benefits on alcohol and cigarettes
articles.summary: The proposals would also see benefits cut for people who are able to work but have failed to hold down a job.
articles.body:
The Conservatives have promised to prevent long-term jobless benefit claimants from spending their welfare payments on alcohol, cigarettes and gambling.

Under the party's proposals, claimants who have been unemployed for more than six months would see their Universal Credit cut by 30% if they have not previously paid enough into the system, despite being able to work.

This reduced rate would be paid onto a "Back to Work" card, which would not allow cash withdrawals or spending on these items.

The Tories said the proposals were designed to encourage people back into work and cut the soaring welfare bill but Labour branded the scheme "unworkable".

A Labour Party spokesperson said: "The Conservatives had 14 years to fix our welfare system but they completely failed to make meaningful reforms.

"Now they are proposing an unworkable new card scheme, which does nothing to tackle the numbers of people their system left signed off and written off."

It's too easy to claim benefits in UK, Badenoch says

Reform proposes £50bn welfare bill cut with changes to disability payments for millions

The Tories estimate the proposed changes would move about 350,000 claimants onto the lower rate of Universal Credit, saving around £538m a year.

Under the proposals, anyone fit to work would get six months on full benefits to find a job.

Every two years a claimant has previously worked would buy an extra year on the full rate of Universal Credit - but those who have not contributed enough would drop to a new "Subsistence Allowance", worth 70% of the full rate.

The party said this would protect "those with a strong employment record".

For example, a 58-year-old who has worked since leaving school but has been made redundant would keep the full allowance up to state pension age.

Claimants who are sick, disabled or already in work would also be exempt, with only those judged capable of work affected.

The Tories said loading the "Subsistence Allowance" onto a pre-paid card, with restrictions on what the money can be spent on, would ensure taxpayers' money supports claimants with essentials like food.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the current system "where someone who can work chooses not to, and earns more benefits than someone in a job" was "unfair".

"The best welfare is a well-paid job. So, we will be tough on those who exploit the system because the current system is unfair to workers, taxpayers and those who truly need support," she said.

"Welfare must be a safety net for those who genuinely need it, not a lifestyle choice for those who can't be bothered."

However, Helen Barnard, director of policy and research at the anti-poverty charity Trussell, said the proposals were "deeply misguided".

"Universal Credit already falls well short of what people need to afford the essentials like food and heating, forcing people across the UK to the doors of food banks," she said.

"We see people's health being damaged and their ability to find and maintain work undermined by the severe hardship so many are facing."

Reform UK's economy spokesman, Robert Jenrick, said the Tories had left record numbers on long-term benefits and the proposals "won't even put a dent" in the welfare bill.

The Conservatives have already pledged to scrap Personal Independence Payment, the main disability benefit in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, for "low-level" mental health conditions to help cut the welfare bill.

The party also wants to make it harder to claim sickness benefits, which it said would mean more people are required to look for work.

Spending on benefits has ballooned in recent years and is forecast to rise to £408.6bn in 2030/31, according to figures from the Department for Work and Pensions.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has insisted he will get the welfare bill down, for example by tackling but number of young people not in education, employment or training, but not through "crude cuts".

articles.title: US aviation sanctions disrupt Iran flights, push travellers overland
articles.summary: Travel disruptions intensify as Iranian airlines lose access to airspace, pushing civilians towards costly land routes.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – Travel is becoming increasingly difficult for Iranian civilians as United States sanctions shut domestic airlines out of much of the world’s airspace and international carriers continue to avoid the country.

The US Department of the Treasury designated 27 airlines on September 8, covering the remaining Iranian carriers that had not previously been sanctioned by Washington. Major names like Iran Air and Mahan are among those already heavily sanctioned, but have continued limited operations.

Recent designations have also targeted individuals and entities linked to aviation support and procurement in the United Arab Emirates, Turkiye, China, India, the United Kingdom, Malaysia and elsewhere.

Airports and companies that provide Iranian-operated aeroplanes with fuel, landing services, or ticket sales risk secondary US sanctions that could cut them off from the US financial system , Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday. It is the latest attempt to squeeze Iran and force it to make concessions amid the US-Israel war on Iran.

Wednesday marked the expiry of a short wind-down period allowing countries to stop servicing Iranian carriers, leading to the cancellation of all but a handful of Iranian flights to Turkiye, UAE and China.

Aviation authorities in several neighbouring countries that had continued to allow Iranian airlines to use their airspace and airport services would no longer be providing them, including Oman, Azerbaijan, and Georgia. In Iraq, Baghdad Airport was declared off-limits to Iranian carriers, but flights to Najaf Airport were still operating on Wednesday.

Many flights between Iran and major transit hubs in Turkiye and the UAE had already been suspended because of the war and sanctions. International airlines have also largely stopped flying to Iran, with Turkish Airlines suspending flights until at least March 2027, and Qatar Airways, Emirates, and Lufthansa’s operations also suspended.

Iran-based aviation and transit expert Mohammadreza Ebrahimpour said years of US sanctions had already forced Iranian airlines to rely on third countries and work with smaller firms to get fuel or services. Obtaining spare parts needed to keep Iran’s ageing aircraft flying has also become increasingly difficult.

But the decision by aviation authorities in neighbouring countries to formally refuse services to Iranian airlines constituted “a new level of sanctions in action” that could have longer-lasting consequences, he told Al Jazeera.

Ebrahimpour said the US had also effectively prohibited international airlines from flying through Iranian airspace by suspending authorisations for some US-origin aircraft to fly to Iran and limiting US-linked overflight payments.

“This is a big blow because payments for overflights were one of the most lucrative parts of [Iran’s] aviation industry, which could act as a support for developing infrastructure and the overall industry,” Ebrahimpour said, adding that Iran earned more than $300m a year from this.

Beyond the effect on civilian passengers and the import of some goods, the measures could put tens of thousands of jobs at risk across the aviation sector and related industries, including tourism and hospitality.

Ebrahimpour pointed out that the International Civil Aviation Agency and other organisations have failed to offer any tangible protection to Iran’s aviation industry during years of sanctions. Iranian authorities, he said, would likely consider China and Russia among the few countries potentially able to provide assistance.

The two countries have rejected US sanctions against Iran, although some of their more globally connected financial networks and companies have, at times, distanced themselves from Iran to avoid secondary sanctions.

The flight cancellations have pushed thousands of travellers towards land crossings, particularly those with Turkiye and Armenia, where onward international flights remain available for Iranians. Heavy congestion has been reported in recent days at the Bazargan and Razi border crossings with Turkiye and along land routes to the Armenian capital Yerevan.

But everyday passenger travel overland into Azerbaijan remains restricted, with Azerbaijan’s government citing internal security and COVID-19 restrictions. As a result, Iranians cannot cross overland into Azerbaijan to catch a flight there.

The Shalamcheh and Chazabeh border crossings with Iraq were also temporarily closed earlier this month, leaving travellers stranded, before reopening to passengers on September 13.

For thousands of Iranians attempting to travel, the flight suspensions mean significantly longer journeys. Some members of the Iranian diaspora have expressed concern online that the lingering effects of war and sanctions could potentially prevent them from visiting parents and other family members in Iran.

Bus tickets from Iran to Turkiye have reportedly sold for quadruple their normal price on the black market amid surging demand.

Some of the people making the journey are young Iranians who are attempting to take international language tests that are not allowed to be administered inside Iran due to sanctions. The tests are often a prerequisite for anyone planning to study, work, or settle abroad.

Iranian academics have also expressed concern about growing isolation from the international academic community. Numerous universities across the globe, including in Norway, Australia, Singapore, Estonia and elsewhere, have in recent weeks rejected postgraduate and research applications from Iranians as a result of US education sanctions.

At the same time, many of Iran’s roughly 90 million people are currently unable to afford international travel – or even domestic flights – as the country’s economic conditions worsen .

The Trump administration has portrayed the war and sanctions as measures directed at the Iranian authorities.

The US Treasury has said its aviation restrictions are intended to disrupt the use of Iranian commercial aviation for weapons procurement and transportation, including activities linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). But the designation of entire airlines under “Operation Economic Outcast”, after nearly seven months of war, has also had sweeping consequences for affected civilians.

Iran’s international aviation network was already badly damaged prior to the latest package of sanctions. Aviation analytics company Cirium reported that international capacity in August 2026 was 49 percent lower than in August 2025, despite a modest recovery from July.

The latest flight cancellations are also expected to further disrupt imports by air at a time when the US naval blockade of Iran’s southern ports in the Strait of Hormuz has constrained maritime trade routes, while war and sanctions have caused disruptions and delays to road and rail cargo routes.

Some of Iran’s medical imports enter the country by air, raising concerns that the latest aviation restrictions could place more pressure on an already struggling healthcare sector . A domestic pharmaceutical company executive told Al Jazeera earlier this month that the cost of some imported supplies, some of which arrived by air, had risen as much as 10-fold as a result of sanctions, wider economic pressure, and war damage.

Addressing the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accused the Trump administration of “bullying”.

“They have tested Iran’s resilience, and now they know full well that Iran cannot be forced to surrender through war,” Pezeshkian said.

articles.title: Federal authorities investigating attorney, accountant linked to Epstein’s estate, source says
articles.summary: The lawyer, Darren Indyke, and the accountant, Richard Kahn, are administrators and executors of Jeffrey Epstein’s estate.
articles.body: Federal authorities have opened an investigation into Jeffrey Epstein’s former attorney and accountant, a senior law enforcement official familiar with the probe told NBC News on Tuesday. The lawyer, Darren Indyke, and the accountant, Richard Kahn, are administrators and executors of Epstein’s estate. Interviews with witnesses have been ongoing, according to the law enforcement official, who could not confirm potential charges or allegations under review or a possible timeline for the case. The Justice Department said in a statement that “we don’t comment on the existence, or lack thereof, of investigations. We have always said with regard to Epstein that if the evidence presents itself, we will investigate.” Daniel Ruzumna, an attorney for Indyke and Kahn, said in a statement that the two had not been subpoenaed or asked to speak with federal prosecutors and have not been told they are the subjects or targets of any investigation. The focus and scope of the investigation were unclear, he said. The Wall Street Journal first reported the probe. Ruzumna said his clients are aware that federal prosecutors recently asked to speak with at least one person who “provided services” to Epstein. He pointed to documents released in connection with the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which President Donald Trump signed last year, and said the documents showed that federal prosecutors did not consider Indyke and Kahn to be among Epstein’s potential co-conspirators during an investigation in 2018 and 2019. Epstein died by suicide in 2019 at the Metropolitan Correctional Center in New York City, where he was jailed awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges. The U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York, which had been in the process of prosecuting Epstein when he died and secured a conviction against accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, declined to comment. Indyke and Kahn testified before the House Oversight Committee this year, Ruzumna said, and have given depositions in multiple lawsuits related to Epstein. “Not a single individual has ever accused Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn of sexual abuse or trafficking, and they reject any suggestion that they were complicit in or in any way knowingly facilitated Mr. Epstein’s sexual abuse or trafficking — conduct that by all accounts occurred behind closed doors, in secluded locations, and at times when neither Mr. Indyke nor Mr. Kahn was present,” Ruzumna said. Last week, the two men were named as defendants in their capacity as executors of his will in a lawsuit filed in federal court. Two women who say their photos were found in Epstein’s collection of sexually explicit images of children sued, saying they want Epstein’s estate to preserve and account for everything seized from his properties. “We want a real, court-supervised process to identify and notify every survivor depicted in that collection,” said the attorney, Hillary Nappi. “Many of them have no idea their images exist in his files, and they deserve to know, and they deserve the chance to seek justice.” An attorney for Indyke and Kahn said Wednesday that the lawsuit names them only in their capacity as co-executors of the Epstein estate, not as individuals.
