articles.title: UK survivor of Canadian poison seller says he exploited her despair
articles.summary: Elisabeth Belien tells Kenneth Law's sentencing hearing she took the poison when she was just 23 years old.
articles.body:
A British woman, one of the survivors of Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law, faced him in court on Wednesday to describe how he had exploited her vulnerability.

Elisabeth Belien told the four-day sentencing hearing of Law in Ontario, Canada she had been at her lowest ebb when he sold her toxic chemicals when she was just 23.

Belien, who until Wednesday had not been known as one of his customers, said she had physically recovered after being successfully given an antidote by medics.

But as she faced him as he sat in the glass-panelled dock, she revealed she had suffered "survivor's guilt" after learning from police others had died.

Law has admitted 14 counts of aiding suicides in Canada after meeting people in suicide forums online. But there are almost 80 deaths in the UK that have also been linked to him.

As part of a plea deal with Canadian authorities, Law will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths.

But impact statements from their families are being read during the sentencing hearing this week.

Man who sold toxic chemicals should rot in hell, says mother of woman who killed herself

Belien told the court: "I had struggled with my mental health for a long time before this. Kenneth Law made it a lot easier to act on that despair.

"I continue to struggle with intrusive thoughts and flashbacks of that day.

"I made a full recovery. However, emotionally and psychologically, the effects are far more long lasting.

"I feel guilty for surviving. Although I survived It has also impacted my loved ones. I feel like my vulnerability was exploited. I still feel a lot of shame about what happened.

"I felt like the purchasing from Kenneth Law, I enabled him to continue his business, supplying his products, to other people who might have been vulnerable, like I was. I felt guilty for surviving."

Belien, who said she took the poison in January 2023, said being in court reminded her "how easily" it could have been her own parents there talking about her.

"I'm learning that things can get better," she said.

"I'm learning to be excited to see what the future holds for me. But the gratitude I'm feeling for being alive today doesn't take away from the trauma of the experience."

Authorities say Law, a former chef, sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients he met in online suicide forums in 40 countries. Roughly a quarter of the packages were sent to the UK.

He was arrested in May 2023, following a complex investigation by at least 11 law-enforcement agencies that involved investigators from around a dozen countries, including the UK, Italy and the US.

David Parfett, whose son Tom died in October 2021 , said in a victim impact statement: "Since Tom died, I've struggled with my mental health.

"Initially, in the months after he died, I didn't properly mourn him, because my focus was on understanding, and then exposing the harm caused by the internet platforms that allowed Law to trade suicide to kids.

"I'm still, after five years, unable to fully process Tom's death. I'm a very different person to who I was before Tom took his own life, having previously been gregarious, outgoing. I find it difficult to enjoy life."

A statement was also read from the parents of Henry Tucker, a 14-year-old British boy who died in October 2021.

Kate and Henry Tucker said Henry had been diagnosed with autism but actually had a neurological condition that could have been treated with antibiotics.

"The realisation that his suffering and his death could have been prevented is a weight that is impossible to bear," they said.

"The death of a children under these circumstance is a heavy burden to carry for the rest of our lives.

"We will carry it however with Henry's blessings until we meet again. We love you Henry."

Norson Harris, the father of British victim Ashleigh Harris, read a statement in person on the agony of losing his daughter.

He said: "The circumstances of Ashleigh's death have been incredibly tough to bear.

"We all feel we should have been able to prevent Ashleigh's death.

"Rather than offer the help needed that individual Kenneth Law sold her a chemical that Ashleigh took to end her life.

"I still hope over time Mr Law will recognise the answer to Ashleigh and the myriad of others who reached out to him should have been that they were loved and there was help available to them."

Earlier Stephen Mitchell Sr, the father of Canadian Stephen Mitchell Jr, told of the aftermath of his death on March 25 2023.

"He was ill, he needed help, and I tried my best to bring him that help," he said.

"Mr Law robbed my son of that chance to be well."

Mr Mitchel Sr, addressing Law in court, said: "I'm willing to accept that during Mr Law's time in incarceration, he might have had brief moments of regret, or even despair and helplessness.

"Perhaps he may have even thought during those moments: my life is meaningless, what is the point of living.

"That was the same thoughts that my son Stephen had before he took the chemicals that Mr Law sold him.

"When my son was well, he would have gladly helped Mr Law work out his depressive thoughts, if asked, because he believed in the value of people."

Sandra Scott, whose daughter, Amara Scott, died on February 9 2022 aged 25, said she and her family were trying to help her through a mental health crisis.

"Our efforts were cut short when, in her most vulnerable state, she made contact with the accused, she said.

"The day I and her friends found Amara, and the way that she died – it broke my heart.

"It was a blessing and an honour to be Amara's mother."

articles.title: FBI says investigating breach of ‘very sensitive’ data by hackers
articles.summary: Hacker group ShinyHunters claims to have detailed data on thousands of FBI employees.
articles.body:
The United States Federal Bureau of Investigation says it is investigating a breach of its jobs website by a hacking group that claims to have obtained sensitive data on thousands of employees.

“The FBI is aware of a cybercriminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the fbijobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information,” the agency said in a statement on Wednesday.

“While the point of breach is still undetermined — whether a third -party or the FBI’s enterprise — we are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support fbijobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk.”

Several news outlets, including Reuters news agency, reported they had seen parts of the data, claimed to be part of a larger trove between two and three terabytes by ShinyHunters, a hacking group claiming responsibility for the breach. According to Reuters, the data includes granular detail about scores of bureau officials’s job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence, drug cartels and more.

ShinyHunters said on Tuesday that it had breached the FBI and stolen data on a huge number of current and former FBI employees. ⁠⁠It said it is holding the data hostage until the bureau rescinds an unflattering statement about the group issued in May. On Wednesday, the group said it was trying to keep the ⁠⁠personnel information from circulating widely in the meantime.

An FBI statement in May characterised ShinyHunters as “threat actors” who often harass or threaten victims, using “their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims”.

The group “may falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist,” the FBI said.

The FBI has been a common hacking target.

In March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. Also that month, a pro-Iranian hacking group claimed to have hacked an account of FBI Director Kash Patel and posted online what appear to be years-old photographs of him, along with a work resume and other personal documents dating back more than a decade.

The jobs portal was still offline Wednesday afternoon.

articles.title: Son of Israel’s ambassador to U.S. critically injured in ramming attack in the occupied West Bank
articles.summary: JERUSALEM — The son of Israel’s ambassador to the United States was gravely injured in a ramming attack in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday.
articles.body: JERUSALEM — The son of Israel’s ambassador to the United States was gravely injured in a ramming attack in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday. Neria Leiter, a reservist in Israel’s military, “needs a miracle,” Ambassador Yechiel Leiter said in a social media post. Leiter’s older son, Moshe Yedidya Leiter, who also served in Israel’s military, was killed in Gaza just days after the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 attack, which triggered the war in Gaza. According to the military and law enforcement, a Palestinian man rammed his car into a security checkpoint Wednesday afternoon near the settlement of Beit Horon, seriously wounding the officer. Israeli forces at the scene then “opened fire at the terrorist as he attempted to flee” and killed him. More military forces were deployed in the aftermath in the area, which is crossed by a major highway connecting Jerusalem to Tel Aviv. A paramedic with the Magen David Adom emergency service said the injured officer was unconscious when crews arrived at the scene and was evacuated to a hospital in Jerusalem. The suspect was identified as Mahmoud Suleiman, according to the Palestinian Health Ministry. Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Isaac Herzog both sent wishes for Leiter’s recovery. A social media post by Herzog described Leiter as “fighting for his life.” Netanyahu visited Leiter’s family at the hospital Wednesday night before departing for the U.N. General Assembly in New York. The Iran war, which Israel launched together with the United States on Feb. 28, is a major focus of the gathering of world leaders. Earlier this week, an Israeli man was killed in a shooting attack in the West Bank, which has experienced a surge in deadly violence since the war in Gaza began. Recent months have seen marked increases in attacks by settlers on Palestinians, evictions from Palestinian towns, Israeli military operations, as well as several Palestinian attacks on Israelis. The latest violence is happening in the middle of the Jewish High Holy Days, just after Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, which is widely considered the holiest day in the Jewish calendar. In mid-April, Ambassador Leiter was a central figure in the first direct diplomatic talks in decades between Israel and Lebanon in Washington. In late June, Leiter, Lebanon’s ambassador to the U.S., and Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced a framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon that was described as a first step toward peace following months of renewed conflict between Israel and the Lebanon-based, Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah.

articles.title: Johnson calls for ‘resolution’ of Iran war
articles.summary: Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is urging “a resolution” to the Iran war, sending the strongest signal to date that Republicans on Capitol Hill are feeling the political sting of the long-drawn conflict heading into the midterm elections. “It’s been a priority and an objective of every administration, for 50 years nearly, to ensure that Iran…
articles.body:
Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is urging “a resolution” to the Iran war, sending the strongest signal to date that Republicans on Capitol Hill are feeling the political sting of the long-drawn conflict heading into the midterm elections.

“It’s been a priority and an objective of every administration, for 50 years nearly, to ensure that Iran didn’t have a nuclear capability. Now that’s done. Operation Epic Fury was an epic success. … The world is safer because of it,” Johnson said in an interview with a local TV station .

“But now we’ve got to bring that to a resolution.”

Johnson did not call for an immediate end to the conflict, nor did he name specific steps the administration could take to wind it down. But his message echoes the calls from a growing number of vulnerable Republicans in both chambers who have emerged in recent days to urge an end to the war for the sake of bringing down domestic consumer costs.

“Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn’t have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran,” Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), who is running for Senate, wrote Tuesday on the social platform X.

She’s calling for a suspension of the federal gas tax and a halt to diesel exports, among other steps.

“These actions to lower costs are needed ASAP,” she said, “and the war needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end.”

Democrats have criticized the war in Iran from the start, and in the final stretch of the campaign they’re going out of their way to highlight the direct link between the conflict and the spike in consumer costs at home, particularly on gas, diesel and fertilizer.

“It’s interesting to me that several [Republicans] who are in tight races, and are on the verge of losing — including in places like Iowa, or Michigan, or Wisconsin — are all now starting to say the war needs to end,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) told reporters Wednesday in the Capitol.

“Where were these Republican sycophants over the last six-plus months when Democrats, in lockstep, have been fighting to end the war of choice in Iran, precisely because it’s not made our country safer, but it has made America, and the American people, economically weaker?”

“That’s the source of the problem,” he added.

Even Johnson is now acknowledging that the Iran conflict has led directly to the higher fuel costs, which have increased the price of other staples as well.

“The Strait of Hormuz not being open affects commerce. It directly affects gas prices and fuel prices. And also, you know, the price of groceries, for example, because they got to be transported, and the higher fuel prices are a factor in that as well,” Johnson told the local outlet.

“Now, all that said, we acknowledge it. We got a lot of work to do,” he added. “I think as soon as the Strait of Hormuz is reopened, and I think we’re entering a new phase of that very soon, then the president’s right. Gas prices come back down.”

articles.title: Lidl banned from selling copycat Birkenstock sandals, Dutch court rules
articles.summary: Lidl must also compensate Birkenstock and pay its legal fees, according to the court ruling
articles.body:
Lidl must stop selling copycat versions of Birkenstock's famous sandals in the Netherlands, a Dutch court has ruled.

The discount supermarket chain faces a fine of €5,000 (£4,200) per day if it fails to comply and must also hand over sales data to Birkenstock, according to the ruling.

Lidl must also compensate Birkenstock and pay its legal fees, with the amount to be decided in separate court decisions.

Birkenstock said the judgement sent a clear message that "copycats must not be allowed to free-ride on [our] creativity and innovation". The BBC has reached out to Lidl for comment.

The ruling, which can still be appealed, means Lidl cannot sell its copycat versions of Birkenstock's Arizona, Madrid, Gizeh, Boston, and Florida models across the Netherlands, after the court found the discount grocer infringed on the brand's trademark "footbed design".

It is the latest in a string of court decisions on Birkenstock designs.

In November 2025, a Dutch court order stopped retailer Scapino from selling similar lookalikes in a judgment which is being appealed.

And in December 2025, Europe's highest court ruled everyday commercial products can hold copyright if they represent creative design choices, a decision which Birkenstock said was relevant to its "iconic" sandals.

However, Birkenstock also faced a setback in Germany's highest court in early 2025.

The sandals may have been cool enough for Margot Robbie to wear in the Barbie film, but the German judges ruled they were practical products rather than works of art – an outcome Birkenstock called a "missed opportunity" at the time.

Following Wednesday's ruling, Birkenstock said it will "continue to defend its rights vigorously and will use all available legal means to combat imitations of its iconic products".

"To protect its retail partners and consumers, Birkenstock will continue to take decisive action against copycats seeking to profit from the company's creative ideas and innovations," it added.

Birkenstock is far from the only fashion brand locked in battles with mass retailers over design mimicry.

Footwear giants like Dr. Martens have repeatedly taken online big-box sellers to court over boot designs, while luxury house Christian Louboutin spent years in global litigation defending its signature red soles against high-street copycats.

articles.title: Allegations of transfer of BCI assets to trust matter of concern: Supreme Court
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court said Wednesday allegations of Bar Council of India's assets being transferred to a trust created by the BCI chairperson are a
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court said Wednesday allegations of Bar Council of India's assets being transferred to a trust created by the BCI chairperson are a matter of concern and it has to be examined. SC also agreed to examine whether it has the power to establish and regulate law colleges and universities.The court was hearing petitions questioning the functioning of BCI-Pearl First Trust and the establishment of law colleges by the trust. It sought BCI's response on the issues within two weeks. A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked how BCI can be considered an expert body to regulate legal education when law scholars and academics are better suited to deal with academic matters. "How can BCI regulate law colleges? That's the real question. Their statutory role comes into existence only after one gets a licence. So the issue is whether law schools can be regulated. We'd like to examine whether BCI has the power to control and regulate universities/law colleges," the bench said.Advocates Prashant Bhushan and Pranav Sachdeva, appearing for petitioner Girish Mittal, said BCI passed a resolution in 2016 and abolished an earlier trust and transferred the funds to a new trust 'Bar Council of India Trust for Promotion of Education, Legal and Professional Reforms and Improvement in Research'. They said the trust established one law college each in Goa and Andhra Pradesh. BCI, however, said the Bar body has passed a resolution providing that there would be no lifetime trustees and that the tenure of trustees would be coterminous with their membership of BCI.SC had earlier said BCI chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra's position was only "pro tem" until a freshly constituted lawyers' body elects its office bearers. Mishra was first elected as BCI chairperson till 2012. articles.body: Kansas Democratic Senate nominee Rev. Adam Hamilton told MS NOW on Wednesday that former Vice President Kamala Harris should stay out of his campaign in Kansas after she traveled to Michigan to campaign for Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, as Hamilton works to win crossover support in the Republican-leaning state. When asked directly whether he would welcome Harris to campaign alongside him in Kansas, Hamilton rejected the prospect. "No, I would not," he told MS NOW. You would actually hurt me," Hamilton said. IOWA DEM GUBERNATORIAL CANDIDATE SAYS HE WOULD NOT WANT BIDEN OR HARRIS TO CAMPAIGN FOR HIM The Republican National Committee responded to Hamilton's remarks in a statement to Fox News Digital, accusing the Democratic nominee of attempting to distance himself from Harris despite what the committee characterized as similarities between their political records. "From demonizing Christians to wanting to ban ranching in a Green New Deal, Adam Hamilton has been in lockstep with Kamala Harris' radical left-wing agenda his entire life. Kansans will reject Hamilton just like they rejected his best friend Kamala Harris in 2024," RNC spokesman Zach Kraft said. Hamilton, the longtime pastor of the Church of Resurrection, won an 11-candidate Democratic primary in August and is challenging Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who is seeking a second term. FOUR MONTHS TO MIDTERMS: 12 RACES THAT WILL DETERMINE THE SENATE MAJORITY He has presented himself as an independent-minded Democrat who must appeal beyond his party’s base. During a CNN appearance last week, Hamilton said national Democratic figures could become liabilities in Kansas because of the state’s large Republican electorate. "I think there are a number of national Democrats that actually would be a liability in Kansas," he said. "I think Kansans are independent-minded, and we've got 45 percent of our state are Republicans and I need those Republicans." KYRSTEN SINEMA QUESTIONS WHETHER MODERATES STILL HAVE A PLACE IN THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY President Donald Trump defeated Harris in Kansas in 2024 with 57.16% of the vote to Harris 41.04%, according to the Kansas secretary of state. Hamilton’s comments came one day after Harris campaigned with El-Sayed in Detroit. The former vice president joined the Michigan Democrat for a roundtable on Black maternal health and health care costs. Harris publicly backed El-Sayed during the appearance and later addressed Democratic voters at an NAACP event. Republicans have also sought to use Hamilton's decades of sermons against him. Vice President JD Vance recently targeted Hamilton's religious and political record while campaigning for Republicans. The RNC's criticism reflects a broader Republican line of attack involving a 2020 Hamilton sermon on climate change. An Associated Press report of the race said that Republican advertising combined separate portions of the sermon, including Hamilton calling Christians to "repentance" for failing to protect creation and, elsewhere in the sermon, suggesting changing one’s diet as one possible way to lower greenhouse gas emissions. He and Marshall both supported a Senate committee farm bill and criticized Democratic senators who opposed it, according to a Kansas Reflector report. Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932, making Hamilton's effort to attract Republican and independent voters central to his campaign against Marshall. articles.title: Australia turns Sydney’s food waste into biogas and electricity; a 62,500-tonne facility can power around 4,000 homes
articles.summary: Every day, food that has reached the end of its useful life leaves kitchens, shops, factories and distribution centres across Sydney.
articles.body: Every day, food that has reached the end of its useful life leaves kitchens, shops, factories and distribution centres across Sydney. Much of it could end up as waste with little further use. At EarthPower in Camellia, that material takes a different route. The facility uses anaerobic digestion to break down organic food waste and capture the biogas produced along the way. That gas is then used to generate electricity, while the remaining material is processed into a soil improver. According to Waste Management Review 2025, EarthPower's upgraded ‘plate to paddock’ facility has a total capacity of 62,500 tonnes, of which 65% is dedicated to food waste expected to yield roughly 1,500 tonnes of soil improver annually while generating enough electricity to power around 4,000 homes.How Australia turns food waste into a resource at EarthPowerAustralia produces a large amount of municipal waste on a per-person basis, and food makes up a substantial share of it. Food waste is also classed as putrescible waste, meaning it can break down relatively quickly when sent to landfill.EarthPower was established in Sydney’s Camellia suburb as a dedicated alternative for organic waste. Rather than treating discarded food as material with no further purpose, the facility takes in waste from a range of businesses and local government sources and puts the organic content through a recovery process.Its intake is not limited to one type of food waste. Solid organic material, grease trap waste, spadable sludge, organic liquids and selected packaged waste can all form part of the feedstock accepted by the facility.That gives the plant a fairly broad role in the local waste system. Food manufacturers and processors, distributors, retailers, commercial kitchens and other businesses can send material there instead of relying solely on conventional disposal.Inside Australia’s EarthPower process for turning waste into powerThe central part of the operation takes place inside two anaerobic digesters. There is no need for oxygen in this stage. Bacteria break down the organic material inside the digesters, producing biogas as the waste decomposes. The gas is collected rather than released and is directed towards cogeneration engines. Those engines turn the biogas into electricity. In practical terms, the process takes material that would otherwise have been discarded and extracts energy from it.The electricity does not all leave the site. EarthPower first uses its own energy and gas production to support the facility's operation. Surplus electricity can then be supplied to the grid for use by domestic, commercial and industrial customers.It is a relatively direct chain: food waste enters the plant, microorganisms break down the organic material, biogas is captured, and that gas becomes electricity.EarthPower’s annual food waste capacityEarthPower's capacity changed significantly when the facility underwent major technological upgrades. The improvements increased its annual feedstock capacity to 62,500 tonnes (65% is dedicated to food waste). At that level, the electricity produced can provide enough power for roughly 4,000 homes. The figure is important because the plant is doing more than simply reducing the volume of material requiring disposal. Its output includes an energy product as well as a recovered material that can be used elsewhere. The upgraded capacity also reflects the range of organic waste being handled. Food does not arrive at the site in one consistent form. Some material is solid, some is liquid, and some comes from waste streams such as grease traps or packaged food.The digestion process creates more than electricity at EarthPowerAnaerobic digestion does not make the entire material disappear. A nutrient-rich sludge remains after the digestion process. At EarthPower, this material is dried using heat generated by the cogeneration engines before being granulated. It can then be sold into agricultural and horticultural markets as a soil improver.That gives the process a second output beyond electricity. The organic waste is effectively split into useful products: the biogas becomes energy, while the remaining material is prepared for use in soil.For a facility dealing with tens of thousands of tonnes of food waste, that distinction matters. The purpose is not simply to move waste somewhere else. The process is designed to recover value from different parts of the material.EarthPower collects food waste from across Sydney’s supply chainThe feedstock reaching EarthPower comes from several points along the food supply chain. Food manufacturing and processing businesses can send their organic waste to the facility, as can companies involved in transportation, storage, wholesale and retail distribution. Commercial kitchens and local government are also among the sources.This means the system sits alongside the everyday movement of food through Sydney rather than operating as a plant for a single type of discarded material. A supermarket, commercial kitchen or food processor may generate waste for very different reasons, but much of that material shares the same basic characteristic: it contains organic matter that can be broken down. EarthPower's system is built around making use of that common property.EarthPower turns biogas into electricity and useful process heatThe most interesting part of the process is perhaps how closely its outputs are linked to its own operation. Biogas produced from the incoming waste fuels the cogeneration engines. Those engines generate electricity, but their heat is also useful. Heat from the engines is used to dry the sludge left behind after digestion. That creates a connected system in which the energy produced during treatment helps prepare another recovered product.The electricity generated on site also helps the facility operate before excess power is sent to the wider grid. In this sense, the plant is not simply an electricity generator attached to a waste facility. The two functions are tied together.Food waste can be recovered instead of simply sent to landfillLandfill remains a conventional destination for food waste, but sending organic material through anaerobic digestion changes what can be recovered from it. EarthPower's process is designed to divert food waste away from landfill while capturing biogas and producing a soil improver. Veolia, which operates the facility, describes the approach as a form of resource recovery in which material that would otherwise be discarded is given another use.For businesses supplying the plant, there is also a practical consideration. Sending food waste for recovery can reduce disposal requirements and associated costs, while the treatment process provides an alternative to fossil-fuel-based energy generation.The result is not a single waste solution but a chain of uses built around the material that remains after food is no longer wanted.62,500 tonnes of food waste feed EarthPower’s recovery systemAfter the 2024 upgrades, the EarthPower facility has a total processing capacity of 62,500 tonnes, with Waste Management Review reporting that 65% is dedicated to food waste. The upgraded operation can generate enough green electricity to potentially power around 4,000 local homes.The same process also produces a granulated soil improver for agricultural and horticultural use. So the discarded food arriving at Camellia does not have one final destination. Its organic content is processed into biogas and energy, while the material left after digestion is prepared for another use.For Sydney's food waste, that turns what begins as a disposal problem into a stream from which both energy and recovered material can be taken.You use AI every day. articles.title: Petition for Sir Tom Jones to return to The Voice backed by Will.i.am
articles.summary: Sir Tom Jones, 86, has appeared as an on-off coach on the ITV show since 2012.
articles.body:
Will.i.am has endorsed a petition to have Sir Tom Jones reinstated on ITV's The Voice.

Sir Tom told his social media followers earlier this month that the broadcaster had "fired" him as a judge on the show .

The 86-year-old singer from Treforest, Rhondda Cynon Taf, has appeared as an on-off coach on the singing competition since it premiered in 2012.

Superfan Aaron Howlett, 50, from Kingston-upon-Hull, started the petition which has received more than 63,000 signatures from around the world.

ITV thanked Sir Tom for all of his years on The Voice and the "countless incredible and unforgettable moments" he gave the show.

Speaking on BBC Radio Wales Breakfast on Wednesday , Howlett said he had been a fan of Sir Tom for four decades.

"Sir Tom is one of the last living legends," he said. "His voice resonates with so many people, young and old."

"If he stopped singing and performing, then he wouldn't be Sir Tom anymore," continued Howlett.

"I think singing is Tom. He resonates from the inside and he becomes alive on stage."

Howlett referenced a recent show Jones performed in Milwaukee, USA, where he "was given a standing ovation at 86".

"He rocked the crowd. He had the crowd in the palm of his hand. He still does it on the television, and he's the reason that most people watch The Voice," he said.

US rapper and songwriter Will.i.am, who has also appeared as a coach on The Voice alongside Sir Tom, collaborated on a Change.org Instagram post on 15 September which shared Howlett's petition.

Howlett said he was "overwhelmed" by the response as, when he started it, he was unsure if "anybody [was] going to follow".

A spokesperson for The Voice previously said: "We have loved working with Sir Tom Jones over the past nine years on The Voice UK.

"While he will no longer be a full-time coach on series 15, we continue to talk to Sir Tom and his team about his involvement in the next series."

In a social media post published earlier this month, Sir Tom said: "They are offering a much-reduced role where I would make an appearance but without being actually involved from the start, and I'm not thrilled about that.

"So the only thing I know right now is that there's never a good time to fire an 86-year-old who's still pretty good at his job."

The programme's 2027 series was due to begin production soon.

In the most recent series of The Voice UK, Sir Tom featured as a coach alongside McFly stars Tom Fletcher and Danny Jones, Will.i.am and Destiny's Child singer Kelly Rowland.

He has also appeared alongside singers Jessie J, Olly Murs, Kylie Minogue and Rita Ora in previous series, and mentored three competitors on the programme who went on to win.

Fans from across the world have commented on the online petition, including Alison, from Peterborough, who wrote: "I, like so many people, watch The Voice because of Sir Tom and will stop watching if he's not on it."

Carmela, from Montreal in Canada, said: "My mom passed away 3 years ago. On her death bed she had to watch Tom Jones on TV and on YouTube. Us Canadians love him. My mom and I went to see him in concert 3 times when he came to visit my city."

An ITV spokesperson said: "ITV would like to thank Sir Tom Jones for all his years on The Voice UK, and the countless incredible and unforgettable moments he gave the show.

"He has brought joy to audiences, and to every singer who performed for him and with him."

articles.title: A Malibu winery that operated for four decades is shutting down after its Pacific Coast Highway tasting room was destroyed in the 2025 Palisades Fire; its owners are now selling the 240-acre vineyard estate
articles.summary: A four-decade-old Los Angeles County winery founded and operated by the Rosenthal family is winding down operations after a series of devastating
articles.body: A four-decade-old Los Angeles County winery founded and operated by the Rosenthal family is winding down operations after a series of devastating setbacks, including the destruction of its primary tasting room in the 2025 Palisades wildfire.According to The Hollywood Reporter, Mark Rosenthal, who runs Rosenthal - The Malibu Estate, has decided to close the winery after years of fires, declining demand and mounting challenges facing the wine business.The winery’s Pacific Coast Highway tasting room was destroyed in the Palisades wildfire, which devastated parts of Los Angeles in 2025. The property was located on California state land under a lease, and Rosenthal says the government has not indicated when, or even whether, commercial tenants will be permitted to return.The site remains fenced off and has been used as a staging and storage area during the extensive cleanup following the disaster, which destroyed more than 6,800 structures.A winery with Hollywood rootsThe Rosenthal family is better known in entertainment circles for its longtime Hollywood businesses, including Raleigh Studios and the Sunset Marquis hotel in West Hollywood.Rosenthal’s father, George Rosenthal, now 95, built a diversified business empire with interests ranging from real estate and file storage to private aviation. Raleigh Studios became a major independent soundstage operator, while the Sunset Marquis developed a legendary reputation as a celebrity haven, particularly among musicians. The hotel was also featured in the 2025 documentary If These Walls Could Rock.George entered the wine business in 1985, when he planted grapes in Malibu’s Newton Canyon. The vines produced their first vintage six years later.The vineyard has since grown into a 240-acre property. Mark Rosenthal described the setting as remarkable, comparing its atmosphere to Tuscany.The microclimate valley sits within the Santa Monica Mountains, an area where vineyards had been established before Prohibition. The region later received American Viticultural Area recognition, and the winery produced cabernet sauvignon, merlot, chardonnay and other varietals.‘It’s been one catastrophe after another’The Palisades wildfire was not the first major disaster to affect the family’s wine business.An earlier Rosenthal tasting room at the Beau Rivage restaurant was destroyed after the building caught fire in 2012. Five years later, the Woolsey wildfire burned nearly all of the family’s Newton Canyon vineyard.Reflecting on the repeated setbacks, Rosenthal told The Hollywood Reporter, “It’s been one catastrophe after another, and at some point it wears you down.”He said the family took pride in putting its name on the wine and enjoyed building the business, but ultimately it remained a commercial operation.“Absent a significant distribution channel like the tasting room, it doesn’t make sense,” he said.Rosenthal said the family had considered opening another tasting room but decided against it. He also pointed to broader challenges in the wine industry, including declining alcohol consumption among younger generations.Newton Canyon property could be soldRather than rebuild the winery business elsewhere, Rosenthal is now looking to sell the Newton Canyon property.He said the property's pastoral setting could make it suitable for a different use, suggesting it could potentially be converted into a luxury inn or rehabilitation facility.Rosenthal, who is turning 67, said he is moving toward what he described as a “family-office footprint.”His transition away from some of the family's entertainment holdings began in 2021, when he sold the Raleigh Studios soundstages to Hackman Capital Partners.Rosenthal reflects on selling Raleigh StudiosLooking back at the soundstage sale, Rosenthal said he had anticipated that demand from streaming companies for production facilities would eventually contract.“There was a little bit of froth in the market,” he said. “I had a suspicion that the demand of the streamers for production would contract.”Rosenthal added that he had spent a long time in the business and believed the market would eventually change.“That was my suspicion, and it turned out to be correct. Whether it was prescient or lucky, I can’t tell you,” he said.Hackman Capital Partners has since faced financial difficulties involving lenders and lost control of several key holdings.Sunset Marquis renovation continuesRosenthal has put proceeds from the Raleigh Studios sale into an ongoing, eight-figure renovation of the Sunset Marquis.He said the villas on Alta Loma have been completely torn apart as part of the renovation, with the aim of returning them to service in November.Rosenthal also expects the main building to be completed by the 2028 Summer Olympics.“We don’t want to lay any of our people off, so we’re doing this project in sections,” he said.Final vineyard tasting set for September 26While the winery is winding down, Rosenthal said the family plans to preserve some of its history through its remaining wine.“We will keep a library of it,” he said, referring to the Rosenthal vintages that will remain with the family.September 26 will be the final day for a guided tasting at the vineyard. Bottles are also being offered at steep discounts to members of The Malibu Estate’s wine club.Rosenthal said his hope is that the remaining wines find their way to people who genuinely appreciate them.“My aspiration is what it’s always been,” he said. “To have it go to the people who will enjoy it and appreciate it.”You use AI every day. articles.title: Xi Jinping arrives in Washington as Trump gives rare airport welcome to kick off US state visit: Top developments
articles.summary: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday for a three-day state visit that began with an unusual gesture from US President Donald
articles.body: Chinese President Xi Jinping arrived in Washington on Wednesday for a three-day state visit that began with an unusual gesture from US President Donald Trump, who personally went to Joint Base Andrews to welcome the Chinese leader and his wife, Peng Liyuan.Trump and first lady Melania Trump were at the Maryland air base for the arrival ceremony, marking a rare occasion in which a US president personally greets a visiting foreign leader at the airport rather than waiting for the guest to arrive at the White House. The visit is Xi's first state visit to Washington in more than a decade.The welcome comes as the US and China remain at odds over trade, artificial intelligence, Iran and Taiwan. The three-day programme is expected to combine high-level diplomatic discussions with extensive ceremonial events, including a formal state dinner at the White House on Thursday.Trump, Melania personally welcome Xi at Joint Base AndrewsTrump and Melania arrived at Joint Base Andrews aboard Marine One ahead of Xi's arrival. The president then moved with his motorcade to the location of the arrival ceremony, where a military honour guard, band and other formations were assembled.The airfield was prepared for a formal welcome, with black SUVs and limousines positioned near the tarmac and the Air Force band marching in formation. Members of different branches of the US military were also present as preparations continued for Xi's arrival.Trump's decision to greet Xi at the air base instead of waiting for him at the White House is being viewed as an unusually personal welcome for a visiting foreign leader. The gesture is part of an elaborate programme intended to match the ceremonial reception Trump received during his visit to China earlier this year.Melania said her husband decided to personally greet Xi because “they have a great relationship.”“He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect,” she said during an interview with Fox News Channel's “Fox & Friends.”Melania also said she had been closely involved in planning the itinerary for Xi and Peng.“Every detail, I was involved,” she said, adding that the visit involved extensive protocol and planning.Three-day visit comes amid tensions over trade, AI, Iran and TaiwanXi's visit comes at a time when relations between Washington and Beijing remain tense despite efforts to maintain what the Trump administration describes as “strategic stability”.Trade, artificial intelligence, Trump's war with Iran and China's designs on Taiwan are among the major issues surrounding the visit. Expectations for a major breakthrough are low, even as the two leaders prepare for closed-door discussions.The visit also follows Trump's trip to China in May. The elaborate reception in Washington is intended to reciprocate the ceremonial grandeur surrounding Trump's visit.When Trump arrived in Beijing, Xi did not personally meet him at the airport. Chinese Vice President Han Zheng was there instead. Air Force One was met by a red carpet, a military honour guard, a military band and about 300 Chinese youths carrying Chinese and American flags and chanting, “Welcome, welcome! Warm welcome!”The children wore white and light blue uniforms that mirrored the traditional colours associated with the presidential aircraft.Wicker criticises 'lavish welcome'The ceremonial reception has also drawn criticism from within the US.Sen. Roger Wicker, the Republican chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, criticised the “lavish welcome” for Xi.Wicker said during a speech in the Senate on Tuesday that Trump should not have invited the Chinese leader “based on all of the troubling issues we have with President Xi and the Chinese Communist Party.”Wicker suggested that Trump could use the state dinner to discuss issues including “the purposes of China’s massive military buildup, or about China’s clear support for Iran.”He also said that “during every minute of dialogue” Trump should keep in mind that “his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America.”Rubio says US must engage China at highest levelsUS Secretary of State Marco Rubio defended the need for high-level engagement with Beijing, saying the United States and China are “the two largest economies in the world” and “probably the two most powerful militaries in the world.”“The idea that we would not interact with them at the highest levels is irresponsible. It’s outrageous. We have to,” Rubio told reporters Wednesday while he was in New York.The administration has presented the engagement as part of efforts to maintain strategic stability between the two countries despite their disagreements.White House state dinner to follow on ThursdayThe airport welcome is only the beginning of a packed three-day programme.On Thursday, Xi and Peng are scheduled to return to the White House for a formal arrival ceremony. The programme will include a review of troops before Trump and Xi turn to discussions on the major issues facing the two countries.The day will culminate in a black-tie state dinner at the White House.The dinner is expected to include prominent technology industry figures, including Nvidia's Jensen Huang and SpaceX's Elon Musk. The broader guest list is expected to feature several major US technology executives.Trump has repeatedly signalled that he wanted the visit to have an elaborate ceremonial character. In recent weeks, he spoke positively about his new helicopter landing pad being ready for Xi's visit while expressing regret that the White House's large ballroom would not be completed in time.Melania and Peng to visit Asian art museumMelania has also planned a separate programme with Peng Liyuan.The two are expected to visit the Smithsonian National Museum of Asian Art, where they will explore cultural connections between the United States and China.Melania said she had been involved in planning the major components of the visit, including the state dinner and the cultural programme for the two first ladies.The visit reflects the broader effort to combine formal diplomacy with cultural events during Xi's stay in Washington.Xi and Peng to visit National ArchivesOn Friday, Xi and Peng are scheduled to return to the White House for private tea with Trump and Melania.The two couples will then travel to the National Archives in Washington, where they are expected to view historic documents connected to the relationship between the United States and China.The White House has said the documents will underscore the historical relationship between the two countries. The National Archives visit will form the concluding part of Xi's three-day state visit.Who is travelling with Xi?Peng Liyuan is confirmed to be travelling with Xi and will return to China with him on Friday.The exact composition of Xi's business delegation was not confirmed in the material provided. The visit comes after Trump travelled to China with several prominent US technology executives, including Apple's Tim Cook, Tesla's Elon Musk and Nvidia's Jensen Huang.Xi's delegation is expected to include business representatives, but the names of the executives travelling with the Chinese president had not been confirmed.Why Xi's Washington visit mattersThe visit is Xi's first trip to Washington since 2015, when he was received by then-US President Barack Obama.It comes as the two countries continue to manage disagreements over trade, technology and broader geopolitical issues. Artificial intelligence, Taiwan and Iran are among the sensitive subjects surrounding the talks, while trade remains a central part of the bilateral relationship.A US-China trade agreement reached last year is also due to expire in November, adding another economic issue to the backdrop of the visit.Against that setting, Xi's arrival has combined an unusually elaborate ceremonial welcome with closed-door diplomacy. Trump has sought to demonstrate warmth towards the Chinese leader, while critics in Washington have questioned the extent of the welcome and urged the administration to raise contentious security and geopolitical issues directly.You use AI every day. articles.title: Trump welcomes Xi for state visit with rare tarmac greeting at Joint Base Andrews
articles.summary: President Trump kicked off a controversial visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping to the U.S. on Wednesday with a rare tarmac greeting at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. Xi’s plane touched down just before 6:00 p.m. EDT, and Trump, along with First Lady Melania Trump, greeted the Chinese president and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at…
articles.body:
President Trump kicked off a controversial visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping to the U.S. on Wednesday with a rare tarmac greeting at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland.

Xi’s plane touched down just before 6:00 p.m. EDT, and Trump, along with First Lady Melania Trump, greeted the Chinese president and his wife, Peng Liyuan, at the bottom of a 100-foot red-carpet. They were accompanied by two children bearing bouquets.

The ceremony included the firing of a canon salute, a 21-person honor cordon, and two three-person color guards carrying the U.S. and Chinese flags. Six F-16s and six F-22s were lined up on the tarmac.

And Xi was serenaded by the U.S. Air Force band playing “Fanfare,” and the American and Chinese national anthems. The event concluded with a flyover of two B1 bombers.

Xi’s arrival kicks off a three-day state visit in the U.S., where Trump’s expected lavish treatment has drawn criticism from key Republicans and widespread condemnation from Democrats.

“I know the President intends to discuss trade and AI with the Chinese leadership — and rightfully so… But, during every minute of dialogue, our commander-in-chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States of America,” Sen Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, said on the Senate floor Tuesday night.

A group of senior Senate Democrats lashed out at Trump’s fawning over Xi at a time when the Chinese Communist Party is supporting America’s adversaries — Russia and Iran — threatening democratic partner — Taiwan — and jailing U.S. citizens.

“As Americans face rising prices for gas, food, housing, and more, President Trump is rolling out the red carpet for President Xi and hosting closed-door dinners so his billionaire friends can strike deals that threaten American jobs and national security,” the Democratic senators wrote.

“President Xi gets the royal treatment while President Trump hurls threats and wages trade wars on allies like Canada,” they added. “This is not leadership, and Americans deserve better.”

Trump’s grand ceremony went beyond the greeting Xi afforded him in Beijing in May. At the time, Trump was greeted by China’s Vice President Han Zheng, among other officials.

Trump’s welcome included a red-carpet with a crowd of children waving U.S. and Chinese flags in sync.

The first lady said earlier Wednesday that her husband decided to host the rare welcome at Joint Base Andrews because the two leaders “have a great relationship.”

“He’s coming on our soil, and we need to welcome them with the most respect,” she said on Fox News’s “Fox & Friends.”

Other presidents who have welcomed foreign leaders on the tarmac include former President Obama, who greeted Pope Francis in 2015 . That honor followed President Bush greeting Pope Benedict XVI on the tarmac in 2008.

Trump has earlier afforded such an honor to Russian President Vladimir Putin, greeting him on the tarmac at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Alaska and inviting him to ride in the presidential motorcade.

The White House frames such engagement as Trump’s personal brand of diplomacy. But some foreign policy and national security experts criticize these actions as providing improper deference to America’s major adversarie and potential security risks.

Xi was last in the U.S. in 2023 for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC), but his last state visit was over a decade ago during the Obama administration.
